accuracy.evidence: Shapes and angles checked against standard A-level data: BeCl₂ and CO₂ linear 180°, BF₃ trigonal planar 120°, CH₄ and NH₄⁺ tetrahedral 109.5°, NH₃ pyramidal 107°, H₂O bent 104.5°, and the measured PH₃ 93.5° and H₂S 92° quoted only as measured values. The 3D geometry code computes the exact angle from the cone formula, so the rendered angle matches the table for every combination.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: reading the flat drawing of CH₄ as 90° (step 1 prediction, m7), counting a double bond as two regions (p5, challenge tag double), ignoring lone pairs so NH₃ is called trigonal planar (m4, challenge tag lpign), naming shapes from regions rather than atoms (m1), giving 109.5° for NH₃ and H₂O (squeeze tag, m8) and counting lone electrons rather than pairs (elec step, p4).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is a rotatable 3D model of electron regions round a central atom: learners squeeze a bond and watch it spring back, turn the molecule, add and remove bonds and lone pairs and see the shape tween to its new geometry with the live bond angle. No other lesson has a 3D repulsion model or this build mechanic.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner act on the rule: release a squeezed bond to feel repulsion, build two and three regions, add a lone pair to turn CH₄ into NH₃ and H₂O and see the angle fall, and work out PH₃ and H₂S from outer electrons. The final sandbox lets any allowed combination be built and named.

predictions.evidence: Predictions precede the action on the flat-cross angle, the shape with three regions, what a lone pair does to the angle and how many lone pairs S has in H₂S. The reveal names the learner's own choice and contrasts it with what the model then shows, so a wrong guess becomes the lesson.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six species are asked with rotated options. Wrong answers are tagged: flat (picked the 2D cross), lpadd (counted lone pair as an atom), lpign (left lone pairs out), squeeze (right shape, wrong angle), double (double bond counted twice) and ion (charge thought to change the shape of NH₄⁺). Each tag gets its own explanation before the 3D model is drawn.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and define each term (region, lone pair) at first use, inside the 6.5 grade limit; adult notes are within 9.5. Chemical formulas use subscript characters so they read naturally on phones and in screen readers.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph gives a count rule, a shape with its angle or a named mistake. Item explanations give the regions and the reason for the angle, and the parameterised items state the computed count in the explanation for every combination.

mobile.evidence: Checked at iPhone 13 size: the 3D model rotates by one-finger drag, regions can be squeezed by drag, and every action has a button (add bond, remove bond, add lone pair, spin). Labels and angle readouts scale with the canvas width and the controls wrap without horizontal scroll.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no violations on any step in dark and light themes at desktop and phone sizes. The canvas aria-label states the current bonds, lone pairs, shape and angle, the status line announces feedback, and every drag has a button alternative so the lab works by keyboard alone.
